To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the BG is a modulatory system, and that phasic DA modulates BG function during learning.
dopamine depletion and overdose in the BG can explain both frontal and implicit learning deficits, and that these deficits can be alleviated by a model-based therapy.

dopamine (DA) dynamically modulates the basal ganglia, which is itself an adaptive modulatory system, and that this DA modulation in the basal ganglion can account for both frontal-like and motor learning impairments in Parkinson's patients.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the neural basis of learning and memory.
understanding the computational function of the basal ganglia and the role of dopamine in its function, and how this function is altered by Parkinson's disease and its treatment.

understanding the neural basis of cognitive dysfunction in Parkinsonism and the effects of dopaminergic medication, and with developing a neurocomputational account of BG/DA dynamics in cognitive control.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the basal ganglia is the main structure involved in the control of movement and the selection of actions in the brain, and that it plays a key role in the control of the prefrontal areas, the areas of the brain involved in the planning and execution of complex actions, and in learning and memory.
the basal ganglia is a dynamic system, which is modulated by dopamine.

DA depletion in PD causes a reduction in the dynamic range of DA in BG, and this reduction causes both the cognitive deficits in nonmedicated patients and the cognitive deficits caused by DA overdose in medicated patients.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the BG modulates frontal cortex, which in turn modulates the BG.
dopamine is a modulator of modulators.
dopamine is an important modulator of cognitive function, and that its role can be understood by considering the dynamic modulation of the basal ganglia.
The main takeaway from our work is that
DA modulation of BG function is a critical component of the cognitive architecture of the BG, and that this modulation is dynamic in nature.

a single dysfunction of DA in the basal ganglion can explain a broad range of cognitive deficits observed in Parkinson's patients, and that the same mechanism can explain why some of the deficits are alleviated with medication while others are not.
the BG is not just a motor system but also plays a critical role in the cognitive domain.
